key_insight: This paper shows that large language models can be trained to propose exact structural edits that make drug-like molecules more synthesizable, instead of generating entirely new compounds. The approach improves over traditional methods while better preserving important molecular features.
problem_solved: Computational drug design often produces molecules that look promising on paper but are hard or impossible to synthesize in the lab. The paper addresses how to reliably edit such molecules into synthesizable versions without losing their useful properties.
method: Train a large language model to predict sequences of molecular edits rather than only final optimized molecules.
Use edit-guidance to transform unsynthesizable candidates into more practical structures while retaining key substructures.
Compare against traditional optimization baselines and show stronger performance in synthesizability and feature preservation.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners in chemistry, this offers a more controllable and practical way to optimize molecules. It suggests language-model-based edit planning can be a powerful alternative to unconstrained generative design when synthesis feasibility matters.
visual_elements: Before-and-after molecule diagram showing unsynthesizable vs. edited synthesizable structure

Performance chart comparing the proposed method with traditional baselines
Highlighted substructure overlay showing preserved key functional groups
paper_title: Guiding large language models to predict edit sequences for molecular synthesizability optimization
